title: Love poured out (Romans 5:5–8)
hook: the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, while we were yet sinners

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification, and the declaration signed in Augsburg. Your line was all have sinned, all are loved. Did you catch yourself ranking anyone? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Would you die for a stranger? Most of us hope we'd be brave, but we don't really know. Would you die for a good person, someone kind, someone you admire? Maybe. Paul thinks about this out loud in Romans 5, almost like a man doing math on a napkin. And then he lands on something that doesn't add up at all: someone who died for people who weren't good, and weren't his friends yet.
screen: `WOULD YOU DIE FOR A STRANGER?` → `FOR A GOOD PERSON, MAYBE.` → `THE MATH THAT DOESN'T ADD UP.`

segments.voice: Start with the image in verse five. In the Douay-Rheims: "the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us." Charity is the old English word for love, the Latin caritas, the Greek agape. And it's poured. Not measured out in spoonfuls, not earned drop by drop. Poured, like water from a jug, until it runs over. Paul says this is why hope doesn't disappoint: the love is already inside, given. Then the napkin math. Scarcely, he says, would anyone die for a righteous man; maybe for a good man someone might dare to die. But then, in the Douay-Rheims: "God commendeth his charity towards us; because when as yet we were sinners, according to the time, Christ died for us." When as yet we were sinners: or, in the older English many people know, while we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up. Not once we deserved it. While we were still a mess, still far off, still not his friends. That's the order Paul insists on: love first, then change. Not change first, then love. Catholics speak of this as grace, a gift given before any merit, and the Catechism quotes verse five when it calls love the Holy Spirit's first gift. Notice what it does to the way you look in the mirror. Your worst day was not a day you were unloved. And notice what it does to how you look at other people: no one you meet is outside the reach of while we were yet sinners. The love came first. That's the whole point of the word poured.
screen: `CARITAS, AGAPE: LOVE.` · `POURED, NOT MEASURED.` · `SCARCELY FOR A RIGHTEOUS MAN.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `LOVE FIRST, THEN CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive love you didn't earn. This one is harder than it sounds. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone was kind to you when you didn't deserve it. A parent after you'd slammed a door. A friend after you'd let them down. A stranger on a bad day. Let yourself remember it fully, without explaining it away. Then imagine love being poured out, like water, on you exactly as you are right now. Don't fix anything first. Just receive. If you pray, you can simply say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Love poured out. God's charity poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, given while we were yet sinners, before we deserved anything. Today's word.
Your line: while we were yet sinners. Today, be kind to one person before they've earned it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, poured into the soul at baptism, and Romans 5 is among the readings the Church offers for confirmation, when it prays for the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: someone who has wronged you comes to you in need, before any apology. what do you do?
options: help, but remind them what they did.
fork.reveal: not graded. but the pattern Paul describes is love first, while we were yet sinners, and change afterward.

original.note: Greek: love, the self-giving love Paul says is poured into our hearts. the Latin is caritas, charity.

trapdoor: what you thought: God loves good people.
what it means: God's love was poured out first, while we were still sinners, not as a reward for becoming good.
what a scholar hears: the verb ekkechutai, poured out, is a perfect tense: it has been poured, and it remains. the same verb is used of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost in Acts 2.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Romans 5:5 and KJV of Romans 5:8.
Catechism references for Romans 5:5 (CCC 733 cites it; 1266 on baptismal grace): confirm.
Ekkechutai (perfect passive of ekcheō) and the same verb in Acts 2:17, 33: confirm.

Reviewer removed 'often read at Pentecost' from howItsDone (Romans 5 is not a standard Pentecost reading; Romans 5:1–5 is read on Trinity Sunday, Year C). Confirm Romans 5 is among the ritual's options for confirmation.

Reviewer changed 'the Catechism links this very verse to the Holy Spirit poured out in baptism' to 'quotes this very verse when it calls love the Holy Spirit's first gift' (CCC 733); confirm, and check whether CCC 1266 should stay in sources.
'Poured once and still filling' reads a lot into the perfect tense; a Keeper may prefer 'has been poured and remains'.

Audit (second sample): Romans 5:8 was quoted from the King James on the Catholic path; it is now quoted from the Douay-Rheims, and the carry's familiar wording 'while we were yet sinners' is given unquoted. 'This very verse' (ambiguous right after verse 8) now says the Catechism quotes verse five; the trapdoor's 'poured once and still filling' is softened.
